entry.title: EMNLP 2026 Budapest.
entry.content:
EMNLP 2026 Reflections on Hungary and AI

I just got back from EMNLP 2026 which was in Budapest. My wife and I are both unfortunately Covid-positive, so I’m writing this feeling under the weather. We came back to very busy lives and being sick, of course, does not help. 

Was it worth it though? Absolutely. Budapest was amazing and I learned so much at the conference. In this blog, I will attempt to do a bit of everything (e.g., reflect on Hungary, talk about trends in NLP research, personal reflections on the changing times, etc.)

Let’s start with Hungary. 

What a beautiful country. There is so much history. Of course, there is history everywhere, but in Hungary, so much of it is still visible. As a comparison, the United States is only 250 years old, and much of the culture, history, and artifacts of the peoples who lived there before European settlement were destroyed or displaced during the “great” westward expansion. Hungary, on the other hand, has endured for centuries. The buildings are eye-candy. Lushes old buildings with mind-bending architecture. There isn’t anything quite like it in the states. Also, the public transportation was also incredibly easy to navigate. This was my first time in Europe and I was really impressed. 

That said, I’ve never felt more patriotic about the United States than when it comes to free water, ice, and the ability to find a public bathroom.

The highlight of our trip as a tourist was the sight-seeing package we purchased. It included a Chicos performance in the Puszta Horse Show and a guided tour of Kecskemét. To keep things brief, I’ll include pictures limit my discussion here. 

The Conference. 

I learned so much. Let’s split it into subsections

The First Keynote

In the opening ceremony the keynote speaker, Pascale Fung, divided NLP/CL research into four major eras, and suggested a throughline for the era we are in today (I’m simplifying a bit here, but I think capture the main idea well).

Era Period Main approach
Symbolic 1950s–1980s Formal grammars and rule-based systems
Empirical 1990s–2000s Corpus patterns and statistical models
Deep Learning 2010s Neural models and probing networks
LLMs 2020s General-purpose language models
Understanding Now -20?? Understanding LLMs and using them to study human language

  • Natural Language Processing (NLP): Developing computational systems that can process, understand, and generate human language.

  • Computational Linguistics (CL): Using computational methods to study how human language works, including its structure, meaning, and use.

She also emphasized that as the field has evolved, the value (and proportion of the research) of computational linguistics has decreased, while the proportion of papers focused on NLP has advanced.

Towards the end of her talk – which I must say, overall I really did enjoy – Dr. Fung made went seemingly off script and made some statements that caught me off guard. They also received considerable pushback during the Q&A.

We need to understand the difference between competence and performance. When a model can outperform humans or another model on some benchmark it doesn’t mean that its intelligence has increased or decreased. Competence and benchmark performance are proxies for intelligence. They’re not exactly the same thing. Even for humans, we have IQ tests and various psychological tests, but they are not the whole picture… They are proxies for understanding human intelligence… For people who argue that language models are conscious, I would say, just show me the evidence. Show me a benchmark for consciousness that works on humans, animals, and LLMs. I have not seen any of that. If you want to work on that, please go ahead, and do it in a scientific way.

I found this statement bizarre for several reasons.

  1. She identifies an important problem—distinguishing benchmark performance from underlying competence—but stops short of offering a concrete solution.
  2. I found it surprising that a keynote speaker at an A* conference was discussing artificial consciousness at all. What a world we live in.
  3. Her argument about consciousness seems particularly strange. She challenges researchers to produce a benchmark that can demonstrate consciousness, but:
    • She acknowledges we can’t even do this for human intelligence, let alone consciousness. Does that mean we should question whether humans are conscious?
    • This seems to contradict her earlier call to distinguish competence from benchmark performance. She’s almost daring researchers to try to develop precisely such a benchmark for consciousness,

Overall, why did I find this talk meaningful? For me, it was validating. The research I presented at EMNLP had always felt a bit like the black sheep of NLP research. You can read the full paper here, but the gist is that we use language models to play a social deduction game with middle schoolers, allowing us to capture and study the middle-schoolers’ language, attitudes, and behaviors. Through Dr. Fung’s lens, my research was more CL focused which she argued was undervalued and deserved more attention. Pretty cool.

Random Research I Liked and Trends

I spent a lot of time wandering around the poster sessions, talking to authors, and checking out research that caught my eye. Here are a few highlights:

  1. Guard Models Are Overconfident Where Base Models Are Uncertain - ACL Anthology: This paper shows that training guard models as binary classifiers can make them overly confident in their predictions, even when they shouldn’t be. The authors suggest introducing an “unsure” class to help address this.
  2. Murano: Design, Run, and Reproduce Mechanistic Interpretability Experiments as Composable Pipelines - ACL Anthology: A package for mechanistic interpretability with syntax similar to Hugging Face Transformers. I’m excited to check this out. It could make interpretability research much easier, more standardized, and more accessible.
  3. GUI Agents for Continual Game Generation - ACL Anthology: Pretty cool idea. One agent develops a game, while another plays it and evaluates it using a rubric (Is it playable? Does it look good? Are there bugs?). That feedback gets passed back to the developer agent, which makes improvements. I asked whether they accounted for “fun,” which could make for an interesting follow-up study.
  4. MemWM: Memory-Augmented Text-Based World Model - ACL Anthology: I just like this sort of research. I’m not familiar enough with the area to appreciate the paper’s specific contribution, but I love text-based games and want to give this one a closer read.
  5. World Models for Policy Refinement in StarCraft II - ACL Anthology: I loved StarCraft II in high school and still occasionally watch competitive matches. Unfortunately, the author wasn’t at the poster when I stopped by, but I’m excited to read the paper.

As for broader trends, and this could just be a reflection of which parts of the venue I wandered through, a few things stood out:

  • Agents. Agents everywhere. It felt like everyone was working on agents in some capacity.

  • Memory and long-context conversations. Lots of research on what models should remember, what they should forget, and how to manage memory efficiently. One particularly interesting paper conducted a four-month user study with 40 participants and found that better memory benchmark performance didn’t translate into greater user satisfaction. Remembering information when explicitly asked (“What did I eat yesterday?”) is different from knowing when to naturally use that information (“I don’t want to eat anything I’ve had recently”). User studies rock. Cool work!

  • vLLM and grounding LLMs. There was plenty of work in these areas, although they’re not particularly interesting to me (at the moment at least).

  • Interpretability. I’m interested in this area, but I also suspect it’s especially vulnerable to AI slop. To my surprise, my favorite interpretability research was presented by guest speaker Michael Franke during the Language Games workshop (LM Playschool: Improving Language Models through Learning from Dialogue Game Interaction). His talk explored how much language models can infer about the hidden factors behind human communication, such as a speaker’s motivations, emotions, and intentions, based on what they say. I plan on reading his paper when (sadly) time permits.

Socializing

Perhaps, the thing I look forward to most when attending conferences is meeting people. The winner of the Dan’s-BFF Award this year goes to Dr. Safa Messaoud! Congratulations, you win, well, nothing tangible, just my thanks.

Safa and I both arrived for registration very early on Sunday expecting a long line. But registration was near instant and we killed the first hour and a half of the conference talking to each other. Beyond that, we just kept running into each other (e.g. on the bus, at the social event where my wife and I sat with her, etc.). She was very friendly, and interesting! I appreciate it when researchers are passionate about their research but are also interesting outside of their careers.

Safa is originally from Tunisia, got her PhD in the States, and now works as a professor in Qatar. She talked about how she was getting back into the gym and picking up piano again.

Want to shout out the other great people I met!

  • Nata – local to Budapest, suggested I read more Brandon Sanderson.
  • Dmitrii Khizbullin– We sat together during the closing ceremony. Very funny.
  • Yanick Zengaffinen – Asked great questions at poster session.
  • Yejin and Dahee (and a third, I forgot her name!) – thanks for letting my wife and I eat dinner with y’all! We had so much fun.
  • Alejandra Zambrano – Thanks for the board game recommendations.
  • Oteo Mamo – We had good chats.
  • Philip Müller – Most likely person I’d call and hang out with if we lived in the same city. He told me he’d go to my poster and he did! And I forgot to go to his! Please forgive me.
  • Many others! If I forgot I’m sorry! This blog is already getting too long!

What Place Does Gen-AI Have in the Research Process?

There is a dichotomy when it comes to using LLMs in research. AI has made it easier than ever to submit papers. EMNLP received over 17,000 submissions this year, roughly double that of last year. I suspect a large part of this increase is driven by AI-generated research. I’m not talking about using AI to rewrite a paragraph or suggest an appropriate statistical test. I’m talking about using LLMs to automate the entire pipeline.

I encountered these sorts of papers frequently while reviewing this round, and my peers have shared similar experiences. A few initially left me feeling really insecure. I’d wrestle with a paper for an hour, struggling to understand what the authors were trying to accomplish. Then I’d start noticing things that didn’t add up. Numbers in tables wouldn’t match those in the text. The methodology wouldn’t make sense. Or the paper would be full of complicated language without saying much of anything.

More and more, a scientist’s job seems to be as much about communicating research as uncovering new knowledge, yet the slop isn’t limited to papers. At the conference, presenters would read verbatim from AI-generated slides. Even worse, during Q&A sessions, some presenters would ask audience members to repeat their questions, record them, wait a few seconds, and then read back AI-generated answers.

A friend and coauthor of mine, John Schneider, compared AI slop to celebrities getting plastic surgery: “Okay, that is certainly a thing you can do, I guess. But… why?” We need to ask ourselves what we want our science to look like. And why we want it to look that way.

I do not envy the ARR editor in chiefs. They have a herculean job of keeping our community afloat. There are nasty pragmatics to consider. What I appreciate most about my time with them was their transparency, their work ethic, and their dedication to good quality research. Figuring out how to fairly keep slop out of our science isn’t an easy task, but after meeting them, I remain hopeful.

Making matters worse, the explosion in submissions puts enormous pressure on reviewers. Reviewing papers is already time-consuming, and it’s not uncommon to suddenly find yourself responsible for eight or twelve submissions. So, naturally, some reviewers turn to AI. At the conference, I told another researcher that I don’t use AI to write my reviews. Her response was, “Wow, how ethical of you.” Apparently, writing your own reviews is noteworthy now.

So we have this weird cycle. AI makes it easier to produce papers, which leads to more submissions, which puts more pressure on reviewers, who then use AI to review those papers. We are doing this to ourselves!

Where do we draw the line? When is AI helping us do better research, and when is it just helping us produce more research?

There are efforts to address these problems, including stricter desk rejections, policies surrounding AI-generated reviews, and attempts to reduce the number of low-quality submissions. I appreciate that the community is taking these issues seriously.

In the music community, teacher’s offer their students this advice:

Student: “How can I play faster?”

Teacher: “Practice slower.”

Student: “What?”

Teacher: “Slow is fast, and fast is slow.”

Maybe academic research could benefit from slowing down a little. Fewer papers, more time spent thinking, and more careful reviewing.

Or maybe that is too optimistic. With craziness like the [Huggingface hack](OpenAI rogue agent breach of Hugging Face - Wikipedia, and AI’s recent dominance in mathematics, we see how dangerous and how useful this technology can be.

Closing Thoughts

On our way to Budapest, my wife and I met a woman at the London airport who worked at Pixar. There had been recent layoffs (she said due to AI), and she was worried about her job security. She was good at her job, but she didn’t feel that was enough anymore.

She asked what I did, and I told her I was an AI researcher. The mood shifted pretty quickly. I tried explaining that my current research focuses on making language models safer for children, but I got the impression that she’d already decided I was one of the bad guys.

I want to be one of the good guys. But I also understand where she’s coming from. I don’t know what job security looks like for anyone anymore. And I don’t think AI researchers are exempt from that uncertainty.

Look at what’s happening in mathematics. 3Blue1Brown recently released a video discussing the future of mathematics in the age of AI. He argues that there’s never been a better time to become a mathematician. AI can help researchers solve problems faster and spend more time developing theories and asking interesting questions.

But one comment offered a different perspective. The commenter compared mathematics and programming to craftsmanship:

Imagine a leather workman who’s life passion is making insanely high quality handbags… And then not gradually, but almost overnight someone comes to his door and tells him we can make bags 50 times better than you at 1/tenth the price. But don’t you worry, you can make more money overseeing the factory, or selling people on how good this bag is, and explaining that to them… A craft I enjoy doing has been taken away from me, I should be allowed to mourn, I don’t care that I can do something else since I never liked doing it in the first place.

I relate to that sentiment.

What gives me hope is the community of researchers I met at EMNLP. I met so many people who genuinely love their work. People who enjoy asking questions, figuring things out, and sharing what they’ve learned. Despite all my complaints about AI slop, I left feeling optimistic about the people working in this field.

We have some say in what our field becomes. But only if we’re willing to take responsibility for it. That means:

  1. Producing substantive research.
  2. Reviewing each other’s work ourselves.
  3. Rejecting papers that don’t meet our standards.
  4. Communicating our findings ourselves.

Otherwise, we risk giving up the very parts of research that made us want to become researchers in the first place. Do we want to be managers on a conveyor belt inspecting the quality of assembly-line papers? Or do we want to hold the power to ask and answer the questions?

entry.title: Keep Your Hands Up.
entry.content:
Keep Your Hands Up.

Here’s an update on my boxing progress. I did some light sparring, Rico pointed out that I sometimes drop my non-busy hand during combinations. I’ve been trying to be cognizant of this during training, but we caught it on video! Keeps me honest. Going to exaggerate keeping my guard tight (phone booth), when throwing.

Did you catch it?

Sometimes Things Go Well.

From a few weeks ago. This wasn’t a completely fair fight. I was fresh, and he had just done a grueling workout. But I was still proud of myself. I landed a couple of overhands. In the moment I thought I was losing but I was getting some good hits. Looking forward to the rematch when we are both fresh.

Sometimes Things Don’t Go So Well.

This was my first time in sparring getting completely overwhelmed. Here is what I learned.

  1. When you are getting overwhelmed don’t put your head down! You can’t see what punches are coming and that is dangerous.
  2. I need to use my legs when I roll. Got to get down low.
  3. After this fight, Joseph and I worked punishing wide swings, getting out of the corner, and upper cuts.
entry.summary: Some recent sparring footage, mistakes I caught on video, a few punches I'm proud of, and things I need to work on.

entry.title: What I’ve learned (so far) from boxing.

link.title: What I’ve learned (so far) from boxing.

entry.content:
What I’ve learned (so far) from boxing.

I started boxing because I was having a hard time dealing with the stress of getting a Ph.D. It is a lot of work, and you get pulled in so many directions. Classes, research, family, money. Everything seems to get stretched thin. My advisor likes to alleviate my anxiety by joking, “I have enough going on that I’m sure at any point in time I’m disappointing at least one person.”

The tipping point was two years ago. I had been struggling with my mental health for several weeks straight, and I told my wife I was going to try something new. Exercise has always been one of the best ways of managing my symptoms, but consistently exercising is hard. It is a lot to plan your workouts, decide on a schedule, show up, put in the work, and keep yourself accountable.

I was the type of kid who wanted to try everything, but my dad talked me out of boxing. He said it would be bad for my brain (and there is wisdom in that!). But as an adult, I can make my own decisions, and I figured my brain couldn’t get much worse.

On the first day, I threw up. I hated it. I was so out of shape. On the second day, I fell in love.

I don’t just love the sport. I also love the community at my particular boxing gym (shout out to Club KO!). The coaches push you hard but are welcoming to all sorts of people. I expected mostly young knuckleheads, but instead I’ve met judges, professors, other students, construction workers, data scientists. All sorts of people. Everyone is rooting for you. Going in and out of the gym, you get so many fist bumps that you can’t help but feel amazing.

One of my favorite things about boxing is that when you’re boxing, you can’t let yourself think about anything else. But I find myself thinking about boxing regardless of what I’m doing.

Five months ago, I started personal training with Coach Joseph Angle Rios. He really got me into sparring and the fighting aspects of boxing, rather than just the fitness side of it. I’ve learned a lot from him, both in and out of the ring.

Quotes that live in my brain rent free.

“Complaining doesn’t hurt anybody but you.”

I didn’t realize how much I complain until I showed up to sparring for the first time. Luckily, I wasn’t the one complaining.

There was a guy (who has since quit), doing some rounds with probably the best fighter at our gym. The guy was swinging wide and kept stopping the clock to fix his headgear, complain about his mouthpiece, to say the floor was wet, that he had a cramp, etc.

I’ve learned that when you’re in a fight, you can tell you’re winning if your opponent is complaining. And the last thing you want to do is give them that reassurance.

I catch myself complaining in and out of the gym. And even though there isn’t an opponent listening, the lesson still applies. Complaining doesn’t hurt anybody but yourself.

“You get tired on the bag so that you don’t get tired in the ring.”

I think hearing Joseph say this was the first time I’d thought of being tired or out of energy as a good thing. I carry this with me into my research. If I’m tired, it means I’m getting ready for when it counts.

“The bag always wins.”

This is mostly an inside joke to myself. To me it means the same thing as the more famous saying “You got to roll with the punches.” But in life it doesn’t always feel like you cleanly roll under punches. Instead you get hit.

When you’re hitting the heavy bag, you can throw everything you’ve got at it round after round. But the bag doesn’t care. It doesn’t get tired, but eventually you will.

I think life can feel like that sometimes. No matter how hard you work, there’s always going to be something else coming your way. You can’t win every round, and sometimes all you can do is catch your breath and keep swinging.

“Punches in bunches.”

Joseph always says “you throw the first punch to land the second on” or “you throw the second punch to land the third one.” Sometimes the first attempt isn’t meant to succeed, but it puts you in a better position for the next one.

“You have to dig deep and find that find that dog in you.”

This one applies to life a little less. But there is some feral part of me that likes to fight. I like pushing myself both physically and mentally, just to see how tough I can be and what I’m capable of on the other side.

entry.title: First Game Jam and 3d-Game!
entry.content:
The making of Chudly Dies (Again)

This weekend I had the opportunity to compete in the GDSC Fall 2026 game jam. I learned a lot, met a bunch of interesting and talented people, and overall had a great time. While many teams registered for the jam, nine teams (including ours) completed a game for the competition. The theme was “loop,” and it was cool to see how each team tackled the theme in different ways.

If you are interested in trying the game we made, you can play in your browser here!

Our Game

We spent the first hour after the theme was announced brainstorming ideas. Prior to the jam, the artist and I had talked, and she mentioned wanting to work more on 3D modeling. So we started thinking about what we could make (other than just a 3D game).

We took ten minutes to individually journal and jot down ideas, hoping this would prevent any one person from dominating the conversation and give us more ideas to work with. I came up with eight ideas, but there are a few I’d be interested in revisiting at some point:

  1. An F-Zero-style racing game on a Möbius strip. The loop element here would have been the racetrack itself.
  2. A music game. Icons representing different sounds could be dragged onto a grid (representing a 4/4 measure with 16th-note subdivisions) to make musical loops (AKA sick phat beats).
  3. A side-scrolling platformer where the player ascends a cylinder by looping around it (a la Fez).
  4. Some sort of orbit simulation (moons loop around planets, planets loop around the sun). We couldn’t think of a gameplay aspect, though, so we didn’t go this route.

Ultimately, we decided on a different member’s idea: a side-scrolling platformer where player would face impossible levels and have to repeat them multiple times, using their corpses as platforms to finish each level. We decided on a horror theme and asked the artist to model whatever excited her.

Development

Development went smoothly at first. I was able to reuse lots of code (e.g., input controls, commands, states, etc.) from previous projects with small modifications (e.g., changing from an isometric camera to a side-scrolling view).

The biggest pain point for me was getting the animations working. The gameplay required leaving the player’s collider and model behind on death, then spawning a new player. For some reason, the freshly spawned players wouldn’t animate when they entered the scene. This led me down the dark path of becoming a ChatGPT warrior. I copied and pasted errors and screenshots. Nothing worked. Two hours before the deadline, I learned that if you turn off the Animator, then turn it back on again, it works properly.

I was the only person familiar with Unity, and for the most part, game engines in general. I also consider myself pretty new to them because the game development class I took was two and a half years ago, and I hadn’t made many games in between. On the first day, I think the others in my group, besides me and the artist, didn’t have much to work on.

On the second, and especially the third day, the person in our group with the least experience really stepped up. I showed him the very basics of Unity and how to use version control. On his own, he was able to find and fix bugs. I wish I’d shown everyone Unity from the start. It would have “cost” us time up front, but I think their own work and learning would have more than made up for it.

What I Learned

  • Copy-pasting AI-generated code, especially when you are learning, is dumb. Instead, figure it out yourself, or at the very least, explicitly retype the AI code. I felt compelled to lean on AI bug hunts because of the fast-approaching deadline, but I think debugging could have been faster if I had just fiddled with it enough myself. I should use my human monkey brain.
  • Letting artists make stuff that they want to make is 💯% the way to go. The best part of our game was the animated fish. The dying animation especially was so, so funny.
  • Working in groups is awesome. The best results come from collaboration.

What’s Next?

For the last few months, I’ve been slowly working my way through two game development books: one about design patterns, the other about Game AI. (As a quick aside, I find it silly how hard it is to talk about classical AI now because LLMs, deep learning, etc., have taken over so much of the zeitgeist.)

I think that Chudly Dies (Again) did a great job of incorporating the State and Command patterns, as well as avoiding the Singleton pattern (as the authors suggest). I want to do a project that puts the Flyweight, Observer, and Prototype patterns to better use. I’ve made small demos (saving those for another post), but it would be nice to do something more substantial, especially with the Flyweight pattern now that I’ve made my first 3D game.

Our game didn’t have sound! We had a developer implement sound in the sample scene but ran out of time to put it into the actual game. I think it would be fun to revisit the music-loop project as a way to learn about that aspect of Unity.

I’d also like to get a little bit better at version control. I’m a lot better than I used to be, but I still rely on AI when it comes to dealing with conflicts.
entry.summary: What I learned building a game in Unity.
